catalog_locator: p. 4 of 5 (PDF page 4), section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', numbered points 1-3 with their two example tables, plus the note under 'Syllable Patterns' on the same page
catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) 1) "Heavy" syllables are stressed wherever they occur because they are derived underlyingly from two syllables. A "heavy syllable" is one which contains either a (C)VV combination or a (C)VC combination. 's 'bem 'beans' | 'ss's-s 'ka.ti.'no.-na 'egg' 'ss 'na.li 'to bite' | 'ss'ss's-s 'fa.li.-'fa.li.'hu.-na 'new' 'ss'ss 'na.wa.'la.hi 'mon' 2) The final syllable is never stressed unless it is heavy. 's'ss'ss 'lau.-'ta.fo.-'ta.fo 'to run' | 's's-s 'lam.-'lam.-na 'its roots' 's'ss 'tau.-'mo.ho 'man' | 'ss's 'ma.li.'bon 'flying fox' 3) Except where a heavy syllable throws the pattern off, stress is normally on every odd syllable, starting with the first and working to the right. If anywhere, the stronger stress tends to be on the last accented syllable. ... For the CVC patterns, it should be pointed out that the only final consonants permitted in Buhutu are nasals.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive rhythmic stress: heavy syllables ((C)VV or (C)VC, codas nasal only) are always stressed; light syllables are stressed on an odd count from the left edge (trochaic, left-to-right), except that a light final syllable is never stressed; the strongest (primary) stress falls on the rightmost stressed syllable. Net effect: primary stress is penultimate in words ending in two light syllables (ˈna.li, ˌna.wa.ˈla.hi, ˌtau-ˈmo.ho) and final when the final syllable is heavy (ˌma.li.ˈbon).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Implied: all heavy syllables and alternating odd-numbered light syllables from the left carry stress; the last of these is the strongest, the others are weaker (e.g. 'lau.-'ta.fo.-'ta.fo, 'fa.li.-'fa.li.'hu.-na).
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy syllables 'throw the pattern off' (the odd-syllable count is disrupted/restarted around them); final syllable stressed only if heavy. 'If anywhere' hedges that the primary/secondary distinction is weak.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement from an SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet; examples are citation forms including suffixed and reduplicated words (hyphens mark morpheme boundaries), so the domain includes affixes/reduplicants. No statement about phrase-level prominence. Tone and length not claimed contrastive (heavy = underlyingly two syllables).
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Buhutu as spoken at Siasiada and neighbouring villages (Ataata, Gelemalaia, Hoowalai, Ipouli, Mila, Sinalili, Bolowai, Leileiyafa; outliers Sagaafo, Libalei), i.e. the language-level languoid buhu1237 itself (alt. names Bohutu, Yaleba, Buhulu, Siasiada). No dialect restriction stated.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary carries no phonology text of its own: its Phonology page delegates entirely to the Cooper & Cooper Organised Phonology Data (SIL 42229). That OPD states: heavy syllables ((C)VV or (C)VC) are always stressed; a light final syllable is never stressed; otherwise stress falls on every odd-numbered syllable counting from the first (left-to-right alternating), with the strongest stress tending to be on the last stressed syllable (i.e. rightmost non-final stressed syllable is primary).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Per the linked OPD: alternating stress on odd syllables from the left, all heavy syllables stressed; primary ('stronger') stress tends to be the last accented syllable, the others secondary. The dictionary pages themselves add nothing.
new_statements.exceptions: Per the linked OPD: heavy syllables 'throw the pattern off'; final syllable unstressed unless heavy. Dictionary Overview/Alphabet page lists 28 letters (a b bw d e f fw g gw h hw i k kw l m mw n o p pw s t u w y ' 'w) with no stress marking; Introduction, Entries explained, Grammar (links to SIL 61431 and 64144 only) and Download ('Coming later..') pages say nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary's Introduction page identifies Buhutu as 'an inland and more northern dialect of the Suau language cluster', ~1,400-1,500 speakers in the Sagarai River Valley (Milne Bay Province), with outlying villages Sawaiha (Savaia), Saga'afo and Oyamamaniya whose speakers the Suau call 'Yaleba'; same variety as the OPD (Siasiada, Buhutu/Bohutu/Yaleba [BXH]).
